notices.message: The frozen input carries two methods in one population and this action yields no relation between them, so `assignments` is empty by decision rather than by omission. `claim-verdict-audit` audits a delivered pack that already exists: it reads the whole artefact set, settles which carrier's numbering governs, resolves every citation mark twice, retrieves the record each mark reaches, puts one of four words on each claim instance, hunts contradictions by entity and re-derives every count — and by its own constraint it never rewrites the pack, its output being a per-instance verdict list. `reporting-checklist-addressability` builds a deliverable's reporting checklist before the first submission: it fixes the published item table, copies that table row for row into a checklist file, writes the substance of the items the deliverable owns into the document under review at headings of their own, maps the plan's acceptance items, re-runs the protected-content comparison and records the repair. Neither does the other's work, so the two are not one method written twice, not one inside the other, and not two answers to one question.

shared_part declined. The concrete sub-capabilities were tested one by one and each turned out to be generic hygiene rather than an operation the two perform the same way. `reporting-checklist-addressability` Verification: "Re-derive every count the checklist or the mapping states from the artefact that carries it, not from the sentence that states the total"; `claim-verdict-audit` Workflow step 7: "Enumerate the rows, entries or events from the artefact that carries them, not from the sentence that states the total, and reconcile the total against that enumeration." That is one clause of a count rule, shared with most verification work, and it names no operation narrower than both methods. The pointer operation differs in the same way: `claim-verdict-audit` Workflow step 3 resolves a citation mark onward to a reference entry and then to the identifier that entry carries, flagging a chain whose end does not match the claim's subject, population or endpoint, whereas `reporting-checklist-addressability` carries an address from a checklist row to a heading written into the document under review. Different pointer, different target, different consequence. The one pointer the two do share is already recorded as a reuse reference inside `reporting-checklist-addressability` itself: "resolving a row's address to the passage that carries the item is the same routing check as pack-level claim verification [reuse method: claim-verdict-audit | when: a delivered pack must be re-checked instance by instance against the material its own pointers name | provides: routing-chain resolution for every pointer in the pack, with one verdict per instance]". An existing method is being cited there, not a shared sub-capability waiting to be extracted; naming it a shared_part would cost both methods content they still carry on their own.

subset declined, in both directions. The wider method would have to do everything the narrower one does and more. `reporting-checklist-addressability` Workflow step 2 copies the published table whole into a checklist file, step 3 writes item substance into the document under review, and step 5 maps the plan's acceptance items; `claim-verdict-audit` has no step that produces a checklist, writes into a document under review, or resolves an acceptance item, and its Constraints state the opposite of step 3: "The audit never rewrites the pack, and it states no clinical conclusion, dose, indication or recommendation of its own". Read the other way round, `reporting-checklist-addressability` neither places verdicts on claim instances, nor retrieves the record a mark resolves to, nor hunts contradictions by entity — `claim-verdict-audit` Workflow steps 4, 6 and 10 — so `reporting-checklist-addressability` is not inside `claim-verdict-audit` either. Each method adds something the other lacks, which is what rules this relation out.

merge declined. Trigger, inputs, workflow and output are not near-equivalent. `reporting-checklist-addressability` When to Use: "Use it as soon as the plan fixes a study type whose reporting guideline ships a published item table, and again when review findings report checklist items as not found or acceptance items as unmet"; `claim-verdict-audit` When to Use: "Use it on a pack that already exists and is about to be relied on, re-published, or built on: after acceptance, before a dependent deliverable, or when someone reports a number they cannot trace back." One runs before the first submission and again in a repair, the other after acceptance. The inputs differ too: `reporting-checklist-addressability` takes the declared study type and its published item table, the deliverable directory and the plan's acceptance list; `claim-verdict-audit` takes the whole delivered artefact set, the pack's reference list as the routing table under test, and the carriers of the pack's numbering. Outputs differ in kind as well — a checklist file with an acceptance mapping against a per-instance verdict list. They are two methods, not one written down twice.

abstract_pattern declined. This relation needs three or more peers, and the frozen input carries two methods. Even at two, the higher-level pattern would have to be something the peers share: a pointer-resolution pattern belongs to verification work generally, which would make it a category rather than a parent of these two. `reporting-checklist-addressability` Verification already grounds that single operation in the existing method `claim-verdict-audit` by reuse reference, so the upward link this relation would create is already present in the downward direction and needs no new parent.

conflicts_with declined. Two prescriptions have to collide in the same situation, and the two situations do not overlap. The nearest pair is a constraint and a step about rewriting: `claim-verdict-audit` Constraints: "The audit never rewrites the pack, and it states no clinical conclusion, dose, indication or recommendation of its own"; `reporting-checklist-addressability` Workflow step 3: "write that substance into the document under review at a heading of its own and address the row there". Read with each method's own When to Use, the first governs an accepted pack that is about to be relied on and the second a deliverable still before its first submission or back in repair, so no single moment is prescribed two opposite actions. Under the skill's instruction not to rank, reconcile or choose, a pair that only looks unreconciled and is in fact an ordered pair is reported as no conflict at all; the ordering is recorded in the revision notes.

supersedes declined, in both directions. Neither is a later, more complete treatment of the other's situation with nothing lost. `reporting-checklist-addressability` does not audit a delivered pack and loses the whole of it: `claim-verdict-audit`'s inventory of claim instances, the double resolution of every citation mark, the four-word verdict vocabulary, the retrieval and access tier rule, the contradiction hunt by entity and the per-instance verdict list. `claim-verdict-audit` does not build a reporting checklist and loses `reporting-checklist-addressability`'s whole of it: the published item table copied row for row with its own identifiers, item substance written into the document under review, the acceptance mapping and the protected-content re-verification. Two methods that each carry what the other lacks cannot stand in a supersession.
